tip: 'Supracitado' is formal bureaucratic language – 'aforementioned'.
'Se bem que' usually takes the indicative in everyday speech – it introduces a concession of fact.
'Raiz' literally means root. Calling a place or person 'raiz' says it's rootsy and authentic, no frills.
'Show de bola' literally names a dazzling bit of ball play, a football spectacle now used as all-purpose praise for anything great.
'Se eu tenho tempo': 'se' + the indicative expresses general truths and habits.
'Pão-duro' is literally hard bread, and it labels a tightwad too stiff to loosen up and spend.
'Manda' is from 'mandar' (to order); it opens casual commands: 'manda a real' (be honest), 'manda ver' (go for it).
'Estar com a cabeça nas nuvens' = to have one's head in the clouds.
'Partiu' is literally departed, past tense, but it works as let's go: 'partiu praia' means we're off to the beach.
'Dar conta de' means to handle or manage something. 'Deu conta do recado' is she pulled off the errand she was handed.
The 'corda' is a wind-up spring, so 'estar com a corda toda' means fully wound up, bursting with energy.
The '-ão' ending makes a bigger, stronger version: 'ligeiro' (quick) plus '-ão' gives 'ligeirão', a real quick one. It scales up many adjectives.
'Sangue bom' = a cool, good-hearted person – Rio ('carioca') slang.
'A menina dos olhos' is literally the pupil of the eye, the same body-part image English packs into apple of the eye.
'Cara' is literally face, but used to address someone it's Brazil's all-purpose dude.
Highly formal letter opening – 'venho por meio desta' is standard business Portuguese.
'Osso' is literally bone, and 'tá osso' means it's tough going, hard as a bone to chew.
'Vacilo' comes from 'vacilar', a cousin of English vacillate: a slip of hesitation that turns into a careless blunder.
'Não fosse' = 'were it not for' – inverted conditional without 'se'.
'Empurrar com a barriga' is literally to push it along with your belly, shoving a task forward instead of actually doing it.
'Com o pé na jaca' is literally with your foot in the jackfruit, the image for having gone overboard.
'Ter o rei na barriga' is literally to have the king in your belly, as if pregnant with royalty, so it means acting self-important.
'Mãozinha' adds the diminutive '-zinha' to 'mão', a little hand. The tiny form softens the offer of help, a very Brazilian touch.
'Com a corda no pescoço' is literally a rope around the neck, and it usually points to money or debt pressure, not just any tight spot.
'Com o pé atrás' is literally with one foot back, poised to step away, so it means being wary or suspicious.
'Dar uma' plus a verb's '-ada' form makes a quick, casual action: 'uma segurada' (a hold), 'uma olhada' (a look), 'uma parada' (a stop).
'Tiro e queda' is literally a shot and a fall: one shot and the target drops, so it means a sure thing that can't fail.
'Dar um jeitinho' = to find a creative solution – a quintessential Brazilian concept.
'Chutou o balde' looks like kick the bucket but is a false friend: it means snapping and giving it all up, never dying.
'Pano pra manga' is literally cloth for a sleeve, plenty of fabric left to work with, so there's much more to the story.
